They are leaves the battlefield, counters, and [music] target creature you control. Sorry to give you the Dora Explorer treatment, but this is important, [music] I promise. By analyzing these keywords and the abilities as a whole, we can figure out what we want to add to the deck. Because of Haywire's first ability, [music] we know we want to find extra ways for Haywire to enter the battlefield in safe ways for him to attack. And then if we extrapolate on that, if we have extra ways for Haywire to enter the battlefield in safe ways for him to attack, [music] we want to add other cards to our deck that have powerful ETB and attack triggers. We also have the second part of the ability that requires us to sacrifice an artifact [music] or a creature for the ability to even work. So it's an absolute must that we add to the deck cards that make things that we don't care about sacrificing or cards we want to actively sacrifice. And of course we can expand on this as well to add more sacrifice into [music] the deck. Additionally, we need plus one plus one counter synergies. But to even make those plus one plus one counter synergies work, we need to have ways for Haywire to leave the battlefield either through dying or through exile. And that's a lot of things to fit into a deck. It's like a whole eight things. And that's a lot. And to make it worse, there's probably tens of thousands of cards [music] with at least one of those keywords on them. So how do we know which ones to put into our deck? Well, the answer is we need to find cards with not just one synergy with Haywire, but multiple overlapping [music] synergies. For example, let's take a look at this card, Air Bender's Ascension. [music] Air Bender Ascension has its own enters ability. When this enchantment enters, air bend up to one target creature, but it also has the following two abilities. Notice how this card has multiple synergies with [music] Haywire. It has the ability to make Haywire leave the battlefield and reenter the battlefield. But, let's look at another card that has multiple synergies with Haywire, [music] although they might be slightly less obvious. This is Angel of Indemnity. [music] And I'm going to give you the Dora Explorer treatment again. Do you see the five synergies [music] this card has with Haywire? The first two are these keyword abilities, flying and lifelink. [music] If I use Haywire, the counters on Angel of Indemnity, the evasion from the flying and the lifelink will become much [music] more valuable. The third is that Angel of Indemnity also has an enters ability. So, every card in your deck [music] that is meant to retrigger Haywire's enters ability will also be able to retrigger Angel of Indemnity's enters ability. Fourthly, [music] this enters ability recurs permanence from the graveyard, which is great for a commander that is constantly sacking stuff and putting things in your graveyard. Lastly, there's this encore ability, which is an ability that can be activated from the graveyard, which means if for some reason I had to sacrifice [music] Angel of Indemnity to Haywire, this card will still provide me value from the graveyard. These cards with multiple synergies are critical in making your deck function. Because to make a deck work really well, you need to have all your cards in your 99 synergize just as well with each other as they do with your commander. I think a hallmark of a really good deck [music] is to be able to never play your commander and still win the game. Now, let's actually go find some cards. I always start by going through my own collection first, and I find all of my cards with multiple overlapping synergies, just like we talked about earlier, and I just make a big pile out of them. My collection is quite large, so I normally don't have a big issue of fumbling together some sort of functional deck just out of the cards I find. But, if you're a newer player or just if your addiction is not as bad as mine, you're going to use a tool like Scryfall [music] to help you find cards. But, the one tip that I will give is that if you've already gone through your collection and found some cards with synergies, you can then use the keywords on those cards as reference for your search terms. The next thing I do is I go through these cards and sort them into general categories. Sometimes it's hard to know what category to put each card into, as there will be a lot of overlap, but I think about it as if I draw this card, how will I use it in most situations? Once I have these cards sorted, I go through and make my first round of cuts, and I use this rubric to do so. If a card is six mana value or more, it must dramatically change the game state or provide me with an insurmountable advantage within one turn. If the card does not meet these requirements, I cut it. No exceptions. There's nothing worse than having a dead six mana value or higher card in your hand, or to waste [music] six mana on a card that does nothing. If a card is mana value five, it must at the bare minimum provide a dramatic advantage to turn it comes down or be a threat that if not addressed by your opponents, will quickly run away with the game within a few turns. At the four mana value slot, cards must be at the bare minimum powerful and highly synergistic pieces that push your deck into overdrive or set you [music] up to have an incredibly impactful next few turns. Cards at the one, two, and three drop slots need to be useful engine pieces that provide value not just the turn that they come down, but turn after turn as the game progresses. When I'm doing this, I'm also thinking a lot about synergy. Synergy is is I talked about earlier. It's when the abilities on two different cards combine to create something greater than their individual parts. And just as you want your cards to have multiple points of synergy with your commander, you really want to be on the lookout [music] for cards that have multiple points of synergy with each other that you can fit in your 99. And when I see these cards with multiple points of synergy with each other, I really want to make sure to include them in my deck. I do this not just to make my deck more powerful, but funner as well. When all your cards in the 99 have a bunch of synergy with each other, it makes your deck more fun. It makes for fun interactions between your cards, and it makes every game of Commander a little different. Also, when I'm making these cuts, I go through and I take out any cards that I think might be too rude that would keep other players from having fun. In the end, I try and narrow these theme cards down to about 40-ish [music] cards. Not all of those will fit in your deck, but they'll give you a good idea of what your deck's going to look like. And just to be clear, you don't actually have to do this with physical cards. It's actually typically a lot easier and faster to do it digitally. Moving on to step three, getting your card advantage right might be the single most important thing that if you get right, it will make your deck work, but if you get it wrong, your deck won't work. [music] So, how do we get it right? Well, I use three rules: density, synergy, [music] and curve. By density, I mean what percentage of your deck is dedicated to card advantage. I also should probably explain what I mean by card advantage. Card advantage is any card that gives you access to net positive cards. Take a look at this card, Faithless Looting. This is a great card. One mana to draw two cards, then discard two cards. But this is not card [music] advantage, even though it says draw cards. By casting this card, you end up going down one card. For a card to be considered card advantage in your deck, it has to put you up cards. That means it not only has to replace itself, [music] it has to draw you additional cards beyond that first. So, at a bare minimum, two cards. Now, let's go back to the topic of density. [music] At a bare minimum, you need 12 pieces of card advantage in your [music] deck. And those pieces need to be dedicated to card advantage. And again, 12 is the bare minimum. I have a number of decks with 16 [music] or 17 pieces of dedicated card advantage. Now, let's move on to the next rule, synergy. Just as we went through and picked all our themed cards for synergy, I do the same with card advantage. When your pieces of card advantage have one, two, or three pieces [music] of synergy with the rest of your deck, you'll find that you'll be able to extract additional [music] value from both your card advantage and your themed cards. Also, it's just going to make your card advantage a lot funner to [music] play because you'll constantly be finding cool and unique ways to use your card advantage. The last step in making your card advantage work really well is curve. [music] important to consider both the amount of card advantage you get for the mana value of your cards and [music] your overall ratio of high mana card advantage and low mana card [music] advantage. Let's say you're running 12 pieces of card advantage. You probably want about eight of those cards [music] to be three mana value or less and only four of those cards [music] to be four mana value or higher. And any of those cards that are on the higher end must explosively [music] draw you cards. I'm talking the potential of draw five, six, or more cards. [music] Whereas those cards on the lower end, it's great if they can explosively draw you cards like that, but they're more likely to be pieces that draw you one or two cards or consistently draw you a card every turn. Before we move on to step four, I just want to implore you [music] to not skip out on your card advantage. In many ways, I think it's the hidden engine in a deck that makes it work really well. [music] It ensures that you always have cards to play, that you have the answers you need when you need them, and it just keeps your deck flowing and functioning well. Now, let's go on to step four, ramp. [music] In normal Magic, you're only allowed to play one land per turn, which means best case scenario, you're only increasing your potential mana pool by one mana per turn. So, on turn five, you theoretically could have five mana to work with. Ramp is any card that accelerates this curve. The most common ramp cards are mana rocks, which are artifacts that produce mana, mana dorks, which are creatures that produce mana, and land tutors, which are cards that search your library for lands and put them onto the battlefield. There are other methods to ramp as well, but those are the three most common. Ramp is without a doubt one of the funnest things you can do in Magic. It allows you to play bigger things faster. And in Commander, since your life total starts at 40, you often have more time to ramp early to get bigger and cooler payoffs late. Since this is the case, if your opponents are able to ramp early and you are not, you are going to fall behind in the game. So, it's important to try and make sure that you're going to get a ramp card out in the first few turns. We're going to do this by making sure we have enough ramp in our deck. To increase the odds of hitting one of these cards early, I always make sure I have at a bare minimum 10 pieces of normal ramp and a few more if my deck has a lot of high mana value cards [music] or if my commander is high mana value. When it comes to this ramp, typically I err on the side of efficiency. [music] One mana value ramp is better than two mana value ramp and two mana value ramp is better than three mana value ramp. There is, of course, exceptions to this rule. Sometimes the synergy on a ramp card is just so good you have to include it or maybe your deck requires a whole bunch of mana so you run bigger ramp cards that make more mana. And then in addition to the normal type of ramp I put in my deck, I actually add a second type of ramp. I call this explosive ramp. What is explosive ramp? Well, it's something like doubling your expected mana output for a single turn or multiple turns. Each color has their own unique way of doing this. There's about a hundred different ways to do it in green from creatures that make giant amounts of mana to mana triplers and doublers [music] and ways to put insane amount of lands onto the battlefield. Blue has a giant enchantments that let you cast things for free. Red has giant rituals and treasure makers. Black has unique lands, its own rituals, and ways to paid life for mana. And white has smothering tithe. And that's about it. Just kidding, there are ways to do this in white. They're just a little circuitous and require [music] a little setup. The hope is that building your deck like this, 10 to 11 pieces of normal ramp and a few pieces of explosive ramp, is that the normal ramp power you through the early game and the explosive ramp will help you finish off the game late. Interaction is what keeps your opponents from killing you. Interaction is one of those things that the more you have in your deck, and the more efficient it is, the better your deck is going to be. The problem is, if you have too much interaction in your deck, you're not going to have fun, and your opponents aren't going [music] to have fun. What is interaction? Interaction is removal. So, something like Swords to Plowshares that exiles a creature your opponent controls. It is interruption, something like counterspell, [music] which literally stops something from being cast. It is protection for you or the things you have, [music] like flare of fortitude. And then there's an additional category to interaction that's kind of its own thing, which are board wipes, [music] which are cards that kill everything on the table, like final showdown. I'll typically run around 10 pieces of dedicated interaction and two to four board wipes. But, if I end up having some incidental interaction in the rest of my deck, I'll reduce the dedicated amount by one or two. Interaction is one of those things where the higher power level you're playing at, the more efficient it needs to be and the more you need in your deck. But, if you're playing at the lower power levels, brackets [music] one, two, and three, you can get away with running more synergistic interaction.
